sentences: Mr. Speaker, I move to suspend the rules and pass the bill (H.R. 7954) to assist Tribal governments in the management of buffalo and buffalo habitat and the reestablishment of buffalo on Indian land.
Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of H.R. 7954, the Don Young Doug LaMalfa Indian Buffalo Management Act, introduced by my friend and colleague Congressman Hurd.

H.R. 7954 directs the Secretary of the Interior to work with Indian Tribes and Tribal organizations to support Tribal capacity to restore, manage, and conserve buffalo and buffalo habitats through grants, contracts, cooperative agreements, and technical assistance.
The Secretary will also be authorized to enter into agreements with Tribes and Tribal organizations to dispose of surplus buffalo on Federal land and transfer buffalo to Indian land.
Mr. Speaker, I thank my friend, the chairman of the Indian and Insular Affairs Subcommittee, the gentleman from Colorado (Mr. Hurd), for his work to advance this bill to the House floor.
Mr. Speaker, I yield 3 minutes to the gentleman from Colorado (Mr. Hurd), the lead sponsor of this bill and the chairman of the Subcommittee on Indian and Insular Affairs.

sentences: Mr. Speaker, I move to suspend the rules and pass the bill (H.R. 741) to elevate the position of Director of the Indian Health Service within the Department of Health and Human Services to Assistant Secretary for Indian Health, and for other purposes, as amended.
Mr. Speaker, H.R. 741 is a straightforward bill to strengthen Indian health leadership within the Department of Health and Human Services.
The bill redesignates the Director of the Indian Health Service as the Assistant Secretary for Indian Health within HHS.
The Federal Government has longstanding responsibilities for Indian healthcare rooted in the Federal trust responsibility.
The Indian Health Service is the principal Federal entity responsible for providing health services to American Indians and Alaska Natives.
Indian health issues do not begin and end at IHS.
Many of these issues require coordination across HHS, including healthcare access, workforce recruitment and retention, behavioral health, public health, and health infrastructure.
When Indian health issues cut across IHS, the senior official responsible for Indian health should be positioned to work across HHS.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: NATIONAL LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICERS REMEMBRANCE, SUPPORT, AND COMMUNITY OUTREACH ACT
statements.title: NATIONAL LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICERS REMEMBRANCE, SUPPORT, AND COMMUNITY OUTREACH ACT
sentences: Mr. Speaker, I move to suspend the rules and pass the bill (H.R. 309) to authorize the Secretary of the Interior to provide funding for the National Law Enforcement Museum, and for other purposes, as amended.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of H.R. 309, the National Law Enforcement Officers Remembrance, Support, and Community Outreach Act, which provides temporary grants from the Department of the Interior to enhance the community outreach, public education, and officer safety and wellness programs of the National Law Enforcement Museum here in Washington, D.C. Supporting our brave men and women in law enforcement should not be a partisan issue, and the overwhelming support behind this bill is a true testament to that scenario.

This legislation has also been endorsed by numerous law enforcement organizations across the Nation, including the National Law Enforcement Officers Memorial Fund, the Federal Law Enforcement Officers Association, the Fraternal Order of Police, the National Association of Police Organizations, and the National Sheriffs' Association.

In my home State of Arkansas, this legislation also enjoys support from the Arkansas Association of Chiefs of Police; the city of Sheridan, Arkansas, Police Department; and the Arkansas Game Warden Association.

In fact, Chief Gary Sipes, the executive director of the Arkansas Association of Chiefs of Police, said: A sustained national effort to restore confidence and understanding in law enforcement is urgently needed, now more than ever.
Every day, law enforcement officers across the country put themselves in harm's way to protect their fellow Americans.
They make tremendous sacrifices to keep our communities safe, uphold the rule of law, and answer the call when their neighbors need them most.

Here in the heart of our Nation's Capital, the National Law Enforcement Officers Memorial honors Federal, Tribal, State, and local law enforcement officers who have made the ultimate sacrifice in the line of duty.
Nearby, the National Law Enforcement Museum helps share the history of American law enforcement through exhibits, educational programming, historical collections, and outreach.

H.R. 309 builds on that mission by authorizing the Department of the Interior to provide grants to the National Law Enforcement Officers Memorial Fund to expand its education and community outreach initiatives.

These grants will support free museum access for officers, expansion of digitized collections, and broader distribution of officer safety and wellness resources to law enforcement agencies across the country.
I am proud to support this legislation, stand with our police officers across the country, and honor the service and sacrifices of America's law enforcement officers.
Mr. Speaker, I yield 2 minutes to the gentleman from Texas (Mr. Nehls), the lead sponsor of this bill and someone who personally knows about law enforcement, having served as a sheriff.

BLM land use plans, referred to as ``resource management plans'' (RMPs), establish goals and objectives to guide future land and resource management actions implemented by BLM.

An RMP generally establishes land use designations; allowable resource uses, resource conditions, goals, and objectives; program constraints and general management practices; areas to be covered by more specific plans; and other related information.

North Dakota Resource Management Plan BLM determined that its 1988 North Dakota RMP needed revision to address significant changes in resource conditions, evolving demands for land use, advances in technology, updated policies and program guidance, and the availability of new scientific data since the original RMP was developed in 1988.

Finally, the North Dakota RMP implements, interprets, or prescribes law or policy, because it designates areas of BLM- administered land for certain purposes in accordance with BLM's responsibilities for land use management under FLPMA.

The North Dakota RMP establishes a broad framework for land use management, governing approximately 58,500 acres of BLM- administered surface land and 4.1 million subsurface acres of BLM-managed land and minerals across North Dakota.
Our conclusion here is consistent with our previous decisions finding that similar land use plans and RMPs implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy.
The North Dakota RMP implements FLPMA and prescribes policy by designating or foreclosing specific activities or land use on BLM-administer land.

Likewise, the North Dakota RMP establishes land use designations that govern all activities conducted by any person or entity on BLM-administered land and subsurface estate managed by the North Dakota Field Office, making it a rule of general applicability. statements.title: WOUNDED KNEE MASSACRE MEMORIAL AND SACRED SITE ACT
sentences: H.R. 165, the Wounded Knee Massacre Memorial and Sacred Site Act, introduced by Congressman Johnson from South Dakota, would place approximately 40 acres of fee land within the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation into restricted fee status for the Oglala Sioux Tribe and Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe.
The land would be held as a memorial and as a sacred site in remembrance of the Indian people killed in the Wounded Knee Massacre in 1890.
On December 29, 1890, a group of Lakota Indians led by Chief Spotted Elk made camp near Wounded Knee Creek on the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation in South Dakota.
A shot rang out, and the U.S. Army opened fire on the largely unarmed group.
At the time, it was estimated that approximately 300 Indian people were killed.
This legislation and the land it sets aside will memorialize and honor the Indian men, women, and children who were killed in 1890.
Mr. Speaker, I urge its adoption, and I yield back the balance of my time.
